prompt.context: Our client, GoNet, is a US-based Internet Service Provider (ISP) that is considering entering the European market. They are currently the dominant player in the US with two revenue streams: a subscription access fee and by taking a percentage of all e-commerce transactions from subscribers. Examining the European market, GoNet has found that the market is highly fragmented and ripe for entry.
prompt.question: You are going into a meeting with the CEO and have been asked to perform some quick 'back of the envelope' calculations to determine the potential profitability of entering Europe.

clarifying_info.q: What is the competitive landscape in Europe?
clarifying_info.a: The industry is highly fragmented. No information is available about market leaders or trends.

clarifying_info.q: How many subscribers does GoNet plan to capture in Europe?
clarifying_info.a: GoNet plans to capture a base of 10 million subscribers.

clarifying_info.q: What will the subscription price be?
How much do subscribers spend online and what is GoNet's commission rate?
clarifying_info.a: The average GoNet subscriber purchases $1,800 of goods on the internet annually. GoNet receives a 3% commission on those purchases.

clarifying_info.q: What are the fixed and variable costs?
clarifying_info.a: Fixed costs are $1 billion annually. Variable costs are $110 per subscriber annually.

exhibits.title: Math Information (Part 1)
exhibits.shows: A summary table of the key assumptions for the European market entry financial model
exhibits.data: 10 million subscribers; $20/month subscription fee; $1,800/year of online spending at 3% commission; Fixed costs: $1 billion; Variable cost: $110/year per subscriber

exhibits.title: Math Information (Part 2)
exhibits.shows: Continuation of math questions for the European market entry scenario including competitor pricing pressure and breakeven analysis
exhibits.data: Same base assumptions as Exhibit 1 applied to questions about $10/month competitive pricing and required subscriber volumes

framework: Assess market attractiveness: size, fragmentation, growth potential
Estimate revenues: subscription fees + e-commerce commission
Estimate costs: fixed infrastructure + variable per-subscriber costs
Stress-test the model: competitive pricing pressure, elasticity of demand
Identify breakeven conditions and required subscriber scale
Evaluate qualitative factors: strategic rationale, risk, cost reduction options

questions.prompt: 1) Please determine the annual net income (before taxes) in Europe, given the current revenue model and set of assumptions. What is the annual gross mark-up, in percentage?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify both revenue streams (subscription + commission), sum them, subtract both fixed and variable costs, and express margin as profit/revenue. A strong candidate calculates cleanly and checks their numbers.

math.setup: Revenue = Subscription revenue + Commission revenue; Cost = Fixed + Variable; Profit = Revenue - Cost; Margin = Profit / Revenue
steps: Subscription revenue: 10M subscribers x $20/month x 12 months = $2,400M = $2.4B
math.answer: Annual net income (before taxes) = $840M; Annual profit margin ≈ 29%

questions.prompt: 2) GoNet just found out that a new entrant is charging $10/month and capturing market share. Can we lower our fee to $10/month?
questions.guidance: Candidate must recalculate revenues at the lower subscription price, keep costs constant, and determine if the venture is still profitable. Should also recognize demand elasticity implications.

math.setup: Recalculate subscription revenue at $10/month, keep commission and all costs the same
steps: New subscription revenue: 10M x $10/month x 12 months = $1,200M = $1.2B
math.answer: No — at $10/month GoNet loses $360M annually. Interviewer should then ask about elasticity: the market should be highly elastic, meaning GoNet cannot win enough subscribers at $20/month either, making entry challenging.

questions.prompt: 3) With high market elasticity, GoNet will not be able to charge more than $10/month. How much would each subscriber have to buy on the Internet to keep profits at the same level as $20/month subscription fees?
questions.guidance: Candidate should work backwards from required total revenue to required commission revenue to required spending per subscriber. Should then assess whether this is realistic.

math.setup: Target profit = $840M; costs = $2.1B; so required revenue = $2.94B. Subscription revenue at $10/month = $1.2B. Solve for required commission revenue, then per-subscriber spending.
math.answer: Each subscriber would need to spend $5,800/year online — more than 3x the current $1,800 assumption. This is unrealistic.

questions.prompt: 4) How much would each subscriber have to buy on the Internet to enable GoNet to break even?
questions.guidance: Candidate should find the commission revenue needed to cover all costs when subscription revenue is at $10/month, then work back to per-subscriber spending.

math.setup: Breakeven: Revenue = Costs = $2.1B. Subscription revenue = $1.2B. Find required commission revenue and implied spending.
steps: Required commission revenue to break even: $2,100M - $1,200M = $900M
math.answer: Each subscriber would need to spend $3,000/year online to break even — more than 50% above the $1,800 current assumption. This is also unrealistic.

questions.prompt: 5) Given that we cannot charge more or realistically increase online shopping significantly, how many subscribers would GoNet need to maintain the same level of expected profits (at $10/month)?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate per-subscriber profit contribution at $10/month and then divide target fixed-cost-covering profit by that contribution. A common mistake is forgetting variable costs.

math.setup: Calculate incremental profit per subscriber at $10/month, then solve for subscriber count needed to cover fixed costs and achieve $840M profit.
steps: Revenue per subscriber: $10/month x 12 = $120/year from subscription + $1,800 x 3% = $54/year commission = $174/year total
Need to cover fixed costs ($1B) + target profit ($840M) = $1.84B... OR: to match original $840M profit: Fixed costs + profit = $1B + $840M = $1.84B
Alternatively, to just cover fixed costs (breakeven): $1,000M / $64 = 15.625M subscribers
math.answer: To maintain the same $840M profit level: ~28.75M subscribers needed. To break even (cover fixed costs): 15.625M subscribers needed. The casebook solution focuses on the 15.625M breakeven figure ($1B / $64 ≈ 15.625M).

brainstorming.prompt: Qualitative discussion: (1) How could GoNet reduce the fixed costs of investment? (2) Would there be any reason to continue with the investment even if it looks like it will lose money? (3) Are there any other risks or benefits GoNet should consider?

categories.name: Reducing fixed costs
ideas: Outsourcing network capacity to local operators
Leasing existing network infrastructure instead of building
Entering only specific geographies rather than pan-European rollout
Partnering with local ISPs or telecoms
Phased rollout to defer capital expenditure

categories.name: Strategic reasons to invest despite losses
ideas: Establish a foothold in European internet retailing
Grow the subscriber base for long-term monetization
Use entry as a loss leader to deter competitors
Gain experience and brand recognition in a new market
Option value: position for future growth as e-commerce expands in Europe

categories.name: Additional risks
ideas: Cultural and language barriers affecting subscriber acquisition
Highly fragmented market may require country-by-country approach
Incumbent operators may retaliate with price cuts

categories.name: Additional benefits
ideas: Diversification of revenue away from US-only exposure
Leverage existing US technology and platform at marginal cost
First-mover advantage in a fragmented market
Cross-selling opportunities with US subscribers who travel or buy from European merchants

recommendation: Based on current assumptions ($20/month, 10M subscribers), the European market entry generates $840M annual profit at a ~29% margin — financially attractive in isolation.
However, competitive pricing pressure (new entrant at $10/month) combined with high demand elasticity makes the $20/month model untenable, turning the venture into a $360M annual loss.
To remain viable at $10/month, GoNet would need 15.6M+ subscribers just to break even, and ~28.75M to match original profit targets — both far above the 10M base plan.

Recommendation: Do not proceed with the current model. GoNet must either differentiate its product to justify a price premium, dramatically increase subscriber acquisition, or significantly reduce fixed costs before this investment makes sense.
risks: Inability to acquire sufficient subscribers in a fragmented, price-sensitive European market
Sustained price competition from entrenched or aggressive new entrants
High fixed cost base ($1B/year) creates significant downside risk if subscriber targets are missed
Regulatory and currency risks across multiple European jurisdictions
next_steps: Conduct market research on European consumer willingness-to-pay and e-commerce spending patterns
Evaluate partnership or acquisition options to reduce fixed costs and accelerate subscriber growth
Assess specific geographies for phased entry rather than pan-European launch
Model scenarios with higher subscriber counts (15M–30M) to identify viable entry conditions
